etymology: A compound of maid and servant. Webster 1828: a female servant. In the Mosaic law the maidservant is named in the fourth and tenth commandments and given specific protections that had no parallel in the surrounding nations.
biblical_def: Maidservant appears in the law of God at points where it matters most, and the placing is deliberate. She is named in the Sabbath commandment, which means the rest was hers as much as the householder’s: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates (Exodus 20:10). One day in seven, the person with the least power in the house could not be made to work. She is named in the tenth commandment among the things a neighbour may not covet (Exodus 20:17), which locates her within a household’s protected order rather than among goods to be acquired. She is given the same manumission rights as the male servant: And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise (Deuteronomy 15:17). And Job names her in his oath of clearing, in a sentence far ahead of its age: If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me (Job 31:13) — and his reason follows: did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MAIDSERVANT as a female servant — a woman employed in the domestic service of a household, distinguished from the manservant.
webster_full: MAIDSERVANT, n. — A female servant; a woman employed in the domestic service of a family.
MAID, n. — An unmarried woman, or a young unmarried woman; also, a female servant.
In the Mosaic law, a bondwoman whose service was limited and whose rights were secured by statute.
Distinguished from the handmaid, which the Authorized Version often uses in a more personal or honourable sense.
Compounded of maid, from Saxon maegden, and servant, from Latin servio, to serve.
scriptures: Exodus 20:10

But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates:
Exodus 20:17
Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.
Deuteronomy 15:17
Then thou shalt take an aul, and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise.
If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me;
corruption_summary: The Mosaic legislation on servants is regularly presented as evidence that Scripture endorses chattel slavery, which ignores both what the law actually required and the fact that it was reforming an institution the whole ancient world took for granted.
corruption_paragraphs: The comparison that matters is not between Israel and the modern West but between Israel and its neighbours. In the codes of the surrounding nations a servant had no sabbath, no term, no right of appeal, and no protection from a master’s violence. The law of Moses gave the maidservant rest on the seventh day by name, release in the seventh year, freedom outright if the master destroyed an eye or a tooth (Exodus 21:26-27), and protection from being sold to a foreign people (Exodus 21:8). Deuteronomy 23:15 forbids returning an escaped servant to his master — the exact reverse of the fugitive-slave laws of the nineteenth century, and a provision no other ancient code contains. Man-stealing, which is what the Atlantic trade consisted of, is a capital crime under Exodus 21:16 and is listed among the lawless in 1 Timothy 1:10.

Job 31:13-15 is the passage that shows where the trajectory was always heading, and it is one of the oldest books in the canon. Job says he did not despise the cause of his manservant or maidservant when they contended with him — that is, when a servant brought a complaint against the master — and grounds it on creation: did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb? A common Maker means a common humanity and therefore a real claim to justice. Paul completes the argument in Philemon, sending a runaway back not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, and telling Onesimus’s master to receive him as myself.
roots_summary: Hebrew amah (H519), a maidservant, bondwoman; shiphchah (H8198), a handmaid; ebed (H5650), a servant; Greek paidiske (G3814), a maidservant, a young female slave.
roots_lines: Hebrew amah (H519) — a maidservant, a female bondservant; the word of Exodus 20:10 and 21:7.
Hebrew shiphchah (H8198) — a handmaid; used of Hagar, Bilhah and Zilpah, and by Mary of herself in the Greek.
Hebrew ebed (H5650) — a servant, a bondman; also the honourable title servant of the LORD.
Greek paidiske (G3814) — a young female servant; the damsel who challenged Peter in the high priest’s hall (Matthew 26:69).
Greek doule (G1399) — a bondmaid; behold the handmaid of the Lord (Luke 1:38).
usage: Thy manservant, nor thy maidservant (Exodus 20:10) — the sabbath rest given by name to the least powerful in the house.
And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise (Deuteronomy 15:17) — the same release, without distinction.
If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant (Job 31:13) — a master answerable to his servants’ complaints.

etymology: A compound of man and servant. Webster 1828: a male servant. Like its counterpart, it is written into the Decalogue itself, in both the fourth and the tenth commandments.
biblical_def: Manservant stands in the Ten Commandments twice, and where it stands tells us what God requires of a household. In the fourth commandment the servant is given the rest his master takes: thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates (Exodus 20:10). Note the reach of the sentence — children, servants, animals, and foreigners inside the gate. The householder is not merely told to rest but forbidden to make anyone under his authority work, which is a limit on power rather than a leisure provision. In the tenth commandment the manservant is protected from a neighbour’s covetousness (Exodus 20:17). Job places him inside the master’s conscience: If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me (Job 31:13). And the Lord makes the abuse of servants the mark of the unfaithful steward who has concluded his master is not coming back: if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken (Luke 12:45).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MANSERVANT as a male servant — a man employed in the service of a household or an estate, distinguished from the maidservant.
webster_full: MANSERVANT, n. — A male servant; a man employed in domestic or estate service.
In the Mosaic law, a Hebrew bondman whose service ran six years, with release in the seventh.
Distinguished from the hired servant, who worked for wages and was not bound.
Named in the fourth and tenth commandments, and therefore under the direct protection of the Decalogue.
Compounded of man, Saxon mann, and servant, from Latin servio, to serve.
scriptures: Exodus 20:10

But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates:
Exodus 20:17
Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.
If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me;
Luke 12:45
But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken;
corruption_summary: Luke 12:45 traces the abuse of subordinates to a single belief — that the master is not coming back — which is a diagnosis of authority gone bad that applies well beyond first-century households.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord’s parable is precise about cause and effect. The steward does not become cruel first and sceptical afterwards; he says in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming, and the beating and the drunkenness follow from that. Every abuse of delegated authority rests on a practical atheism about accountability: the elder who bullies his congregation, the husband who rules his wife harshly, the employer who treats people as inventory, all operate on the working assumption that no reckoning is coming. Paul makes the same connection in reverse when instructing masters: knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1). The doctrine of the second coming is not an appendix to Christian ethics; it is the thing that makes ordinary daily conduct answerable.

The placement of the manservant in the fourth commandment deserves attention on its own account. The sabbath command does not say the householder may rest; it says he shall not make his son, his daughter, his servants, his animals, or the foreigner inside his gates work. It is a constraint on the powerful, framed as worship. Deuteronomy 5:15 gives the reason explicitly — remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt — so that Israel’s treatment of its own servants was to be shaped by the memory of its own bondage. A society that has abolished the day has not thereby freed anyone; it has removed the one weekly limit that the least powerful could rely on.
roots_summary: Hebrew ebed (H5650), a servant, bondman; naar (H5288), a young man, a servant; Greek pais (G3816), a boy, a servant; doulos (G1401), a bondservant.
roots_lines: Hebrew ebed (H5650) — a servant, a bondman; the word of the fourth and tenth commandments.
Hebrew naar (H5288) — a lad, a young servant; used of Gehazi and of Joshua under Moses.
Greek pais (G3816) — a child or a servant; the centurion’s servant in Matthew 8:6.
Greek doulos (G1401) — a bondservant, one owned; Paul’s ordinary self-description, a servant of Jesus Christ.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a household steward; the office of the man in Luke 12:42-45.
usage: Thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant (Exodus 20:10) — the sabbath as a limit on the powerful.
If I did despise the cause of my manservant (Job 31:13) — a master who let his servants contend with him.
My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants (Luke 12:45) — cruelty traced to disbelief in a reckoning.

etymology: From Old French maistresse, the feminine of maistre, master, from Latin magister. Webster 1828: a woman who governs; the female head of a family; correlative to servant or slave. Scripture uses it of Sarai over Hagar, of a Hebrew captive’s Syrian mistress, and once of Nineveh.
biblical_def: Mistress in Scripture is the female head of a household, and the word appears at some revealing moments. It marks the collapse of a scheme Sarai herself devised: when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes (Genesis 16:4) — Sarai had given Hagar to Abram, and the contempt that followed was the first fruit of it. It marks an astonishing act of mercy from a captive: And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy (2 Kings 5:3). A little Israelite girl, carried off by a Syrian raid, tells her captor’s wife where healing may be found; the whole of Naaman’s story runs through her sentence, and Scripture never gives her a name. Proverbs names an inversion that unsettles a household: an handmaid that is heir to her mistress (Proverbs 30:23). Isaiah levels every station in one judgment: as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller (Isaiah 24:2). And Psalm 123 makes the mistress a picture of God: as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God (Psalm 123:2).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MISTRESS as a woman who governs; the female head of a family or of a household; a woman who has authority over servants; and, correlatively to servant or slave, the female counterpart of master.
webster_full: MISTRESS, n. — A woman who governs; correlative to servant or slave.
The female head of a family; the woman who has the direction and management of a household.
A woman who has possession and command of anything; as, mistress of a house or of an art.
A title of address and respect for a woman, whence the abbreviations Mrs. and Miss.
From Old French maistresse, from Latin magister, master — the root also of magistrate and magisterial.
scriptures: Genesis 16:4
And he went in unto Hagar, and she conceived: and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
2 Kings 5:3
And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy.
Proverbs 30:23
For an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress.
Psalm 123:2

Behold, as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us.
corruption_summary: The unnamed captive girl of 2 Kings 5 is the Bible’s quiet answer to the assumption that only the visible and titled do anything of consequence in the kingdom of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Everything in the chapter turns on one sentence spoken by a child who had been carried off in a raid. She had every reason for silence: Syrian bands had taken her from her home, and the man she might have helped was the captain of the army that did it. She tells her mistress about the prophet in Samaria, and the result is a Gentile general healed, a testimony carried back to Damascus, and a passage the Lord Jesus later cited in His own synagogue to the fury of His neighbours (Luke 4:27). Scripture does not record her name. That is the ordinary shape of usefulness in the kingdom, and it is a rebuke to a church that measures ministry by visibility and to any believer who concludes that a life without a platform is a life without service.

Genesis 16 supplies the warning on the other side, and it is about attempting God’s promise by human management. Sarai proposed Hagar because the promise was slow; Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai, which is the exact phrase used of Adam hearkening to Eve; and what followed was contempt, harsh dealing, flight, and a division that has not healed. The blame is distributed and the narrative does not spare anyone, least of all the patriarch. Yet the angel of the LORD finds Hagar in the wilderness, calls her by name and by station, gives her a promise, and she names Him Thou God seest me. God’s mercy to the woman wronged by a scheme is as real as His judgment on the scheme.
roots_summary: Hebrew gebereth (H1404), a mistress, a lady; gebirah (H1377), a queen mother, a mistress; Greek kuria (G2959), a lady; despotes (G1203), a master.
roots_lines: Hebrew gebereth (H1404) — a lady, a mistress; from gabar, to be strong; her mistress was despised in her eyes (Genesis 16:4).
Hebrew gebirah (H1377) — a queen or queen mother; used of Maachah and of Jezebel’s station.
Hebrew shiphchah (H8198) — a handmaid; the correlative term in Proverbs 30:23.
Greek kuria (G2959) — a lady; the elder unto the elect lady (2 John 1:1).
Greek despotes (G1203) — an absolute master; used of God in Luke 2:29 and of household heads in 1 Timothy 6:1.
usage: Her mistress was despised in her eyes (Genesis 16:4) — the first fruit of a scheme to hurry a promise.
She said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet (2 Kings 5:3) — an unnamed captive and a healed general.
As the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress (Psalm 123:2) — watching a hand for the least sign of mercy.

etymology: From Old French nourice, from Latin nutrix, from nutrire, to nourish. Webster 1828: a woman who has the care of infants, or who suckles a child not her own; one who tends the sick. Paul takes it up as an image of apostolic ministry.
biblical_def: Nurse in Scripture is a figure of tender, costly, unglamorous care, and Paul reaches for it to describe his own ministry. But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7) — and the Greek suggests a nursing mother with her own children, not a hired attendant; the next verse says the apostles were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls. Moses’ sister uses the office to reunite a rescued baby with his own mother: Shall I go and call to thee a nurse of the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for thee? (Exodus 2:7) — and Pharaoh’s daughter pays Jochebed to raise her own son. Naomi, emptied at the start of the book, ends it holding a child: And Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it (Ruth 4:16). A nurse’s flight leaves a permanent mark in the royal house: his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). And Isaiah promises kings and queens as nursing fathers and nursing mothers to Zion (Isaiah 49:23).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NURSE as a woman who has the care of infants, or who suckles a child not her own; a woman who tends the sick; and, as a verb, to nourish, to suckle, to tend in sickness, and figuratively to promote growth.
webster_full: NURSE, n. — A woman who has the care of infants, or who suckles a child not her own.
A woman who tends the sick; one who attends and cares for the helpless.
NURSE, v.t. — To suckle; to nourish at the breast; to tend, as an infant or a sick person.
Figuratively, to bring up, to foster, to promote the growth of anything — whence a nursery.
From Latin nutrix, from nutrio, to nourish — the root also of nutriment, nutrition, and nourish.
scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 2:7
But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children:
Exodus 2:7
Then said his sister to Pharaoh's daughter, Shall I go and call to thee a nurse of the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for thee?
Ruth 4:16
And Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it.
2 Samuel 4:4

And Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth.
corruption_summary: 1 Thessalonians 2:7 gives a nursing mother as the model for how a minister handles a congregation, which sits badly with both the executive model of pastoral leadership and the assumption that gentleness in a man is weakness.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul had every right to press his apostolic authority in Thessalonica and says so in the same breath — when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ — and then chooses the opposite: we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children. Three verses later he changes the figure to a father exhorting and charging his children, so the passage gives both, and neither is the executive. The dictionary holds male-only eldership without qualification; the office belongs to men. But the manner Scripture assigns to that office is nursing and fathering, not managing, and Peter forbids elders to be lords over God’s heritage. A man who cannot be gentle is not thereby more masculine; by this text he is less fit for the office.

The other three uses are worth holding together, because they show what such care costs and what it is worth. Jochebed nursed her own son for Pharaoh’s wages and gave him up again. Naomi, who had told the women of Bethlehem to call her Mara because the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her, ends the book with a child in her bosom and the neighbours saying there is a son born to Naomi — and that child is Obed, the grandfather of David. And Mephibosheth was lamed for life by a nurse running to save him, which is Scripture’s honest note that even faithful care in a crisis can leave permanent damage. The same lame man is later seated at David’s table continually, and the two facts are allowed to stand together.
roots_summary: Hebrew yanaq (H3243), to suck, to nurse; omeneth (H539 participle), a nurse, one who supports; Greek trophos (G5162), a nurse; thalpo (G2282), to warm, to cherish.
roots_lines: Hebrew yanaq (H3243) — to suck, and in the causative to give suck; that she may nurse the child (Exodus 2:7).
Hebrew omeneth — a nurse, from aman, to support, be faithful; the same root as amen; became nurse unto it (Ruth 4:16).
Greek trophos (G5162) — a nurse, a nursing mother; even as a nurse cherisheth her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7).
Greek thalpo (G2282) — to warm, to cherish; the same verb used of a husband cherishing his wife (Ephesians 5:29).
Hebrew oman (H539) — a foster father, a nourisher; kings shall be thy nursing fathers (Isaiah 49:23).
usage: Even as a nurse cherisheth her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7) — the manner Scripture assigns to the pastoral office.
Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it (Ruth 4:16) — the woman who called herself Mara, holding David’s grandfather.
His nurse took him up, and fled… and he became lame (2 Samuel 4:4) — faithful care in a crisis, and permanent damage.

etymology: From Saxon maegden, a young unmarried woman. Webster 1828: an unmarried woman, or a woman who has not known man; a virgin. Scripture uses it of a girl watching her mistress’s hand, of a dead child raised, and of those spared nothing in a sacked city.
biblical_def: Maiden in Scripture is a young unmarried woman or girl, and the word appears at points of great tenderness and great horror. The psalm of ascents makes her posture the picture of the believer’s waiting: as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us (Psalm 123:2). A servant watched her mistress’s hand, not her face, because instruction came by gesture — a fixed, patient attention for the smallest sign, and the psalm makes it the model of prayer. Luke uses the word for Jairus’s daughter at the moment of the miracle: he suffered no man to go in, save Peter, and James, and John, and the father and the mother of the maiden (Luke 8:51), and the Lord took her by the hand and said Maid, arise. And the chronicler uses it in the bleakest sentence of the exile, listing those the Chaldeans spared nothing: had no compassion upon young man or maiden, old man, or him that stooped for age (2 Chronicles 36:17). The Lord also names maidens among the servants an unfaithful steward begins to beat when he thinks his master delays (Luke 12:45).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MAIDEN as an unmarried woman, or a woman who has not known a man; a virgin; and as an adjective, pertaining to a virgin, and hence fresh, new, or unused.
webster_full: MAIDEN, n. — An unmarried woman, or a woman who has not known a man; a virgin.
A female servant; a girl in domestic service.
MAIDEN, a. — Pertaining to a virgin; consisting of virgins; as, a maiden troop.
Fresh; new; unused; as, maiden soil, or a maiden sword — that which has not yet been employed.
From Saxon maegden, a maid — the root also of maid and maidenhood.
scriptures: Psalm 123:2

Behold, as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us.
Luke 8:51
And when he came into the house, he suffered no man to go in, save Peter, and James, and John, and the father and the mother of the maiden.
2 Chronicles 36:17

Therefore he brought upon them the king of the Chaldees, who slew their young men with the sword in the house of their sanctuary, and had no compassion upon young man or maiden, old man, or him that stooped for age: he gave them all into his hand.
Luke 12:45
But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken;
corruption_summary: Psalm 123:2 makes a servant girl’s watching of her mistress’s hand the model of prayer, which is a posture of dependence the modern emphasis on prayer as conversation between equals has largely lost.
corruption_paragraphs: The image is precise. A maidservant did not watch her mistress’s face for a mood; she watched the hand, because direction came by gesture and she must not miss it. The psalmist applies this exactly: so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us. Two things follow. The first is attentiveness — the fixed watching of one who has no other resource. The second is patience without a stated term: until. The psalm is short, and its last two verses say the soul is exceedingly filled with the contempt of the proud, so this is not the prayer of the comfortable. Modern devotional language, which encourages the believer to approach God as a friend and to be at ease, has real warrant in John 15:15, but it is not the whole of the Bible’s teaching on prayer, and Psalm 123 is what it has mislaid.

2 Chronicles 36:17 must not be softened, and the dictionary does not attempt it. The Chaldeans had no compassion upon young man or maiden, old man, or him that stooped for age, and the chronicler says outright that God brought upon them the king of the Chaldees. The verses before give the reason: the people mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and misused His prophets, until there was no remedy. This is not a text that permits any comfortable reading of God’s patience, and it stands as the historical demonstration of Hebrews 10:31. Luke 8:51 is set here deliberately as its counterweight: the same God who let Jerusalem fall took a dead girl by the hand and called her back.
roots_summary: Hebrew almah (H5959), a young woman of marriageable age; naarah (H5291), a girl, a damsel; bethulah (H1330), a virgin; Greek pais (G3816), a girl or boy.
roots_lines: Hebrew naarah (H5291) — a girl, a damsel, a maidservant; the ordinary word for a young woman in service.
Hebrew almah (H5959) — a young woman of marriageable age; the word of Isaiah 7:14, rendered virgin and so quoted in Matthew 1:23.
Hebrew bethulah (H1330) — a virgin; the strict term, used of Rebekah in Genesis 24:16.
Greek pais (G3816) — a child, boy or girl; the father and the mother of the maiden (Luke 8:51).
Greek paidiske (G3814) — a young female servant; the maidens of Luke 12:45.
usage: As the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress (Psalm 123:2) — watching a hand, not a face, for the least sign.
The father and the mother of the maiden (Luke 8:51) — the room emptied before a dead girl was raised.
Had no compassion upon young man or maiden (2 Chronicles 36:17) — the fall of Jerusalem, stated without softening.

etymology: From kin, Saxon cynn, race or family, and men. Webster 1828: relatives; those of the same blood or family. In the Old Testament the kinsman carries a legal office — the goel, the redeemer of a relative’s person, land, and blood.
biblical_def: Kinsmen are blood relatives, and in Israel the relation carried duties that no other society imposed. The nearest kinsman was obliged to redeem a relative sold into servitude, to buy back land the family had lost, to avenge shed blood, and in some cases to raise up seed to a dead brother — the whole office of the goel, which is the machinery of the book of Ruth and the type behind the doctrine of redemption. Paul writes with anguish about his own kinsmen: For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:3) — the strongest expression of love for an unbelieving people in Scripture. He greets kinsmen among the Roman Christians: Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me (Romans 16:7). And the Lord uses kinsmen to overturn the ordinary logic of hospitality: When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee (Luke 14:12) — invite instead those who cannot repay.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines KINSMAN as a man of the same race or family; one related by blood; and in the plural, relatives or kindred. The Hebrew law attached particular obligations of redemption to the nearest kinsman.
webster_full: KINSMEN, n. pl. of KINSMAN — Men of the same race or family; relatives by blood.
KINSMAN, n. — A man of the same kin or family; a relative.
In Hebrew law, the near kinsman had the right and duty of redeeming a relative’s person or inheritance.
KIN, n. — Relation, properly by consanguinity or descent from a common ancestor.
From Saxon cynn, kind, race, family — the root also of kind, kindred, and king.
scriptures: Romans 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
Romans 16:7
Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me.
Luke 14:12

Then said he also to him that bade him, When thou makest a dinner or a supper, call not thy friends, nor thy brethren, neither thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours; lest they also bid thee again, and a recompence be made thee.
Leviticus 25:49
Either his uncle, or his uncle's son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself.
corruption_summary: Romans 16:7 is regularly produced as proof that a woman held apostolic office, which requires both a disputed reading of the name and a disputed sense of a phrase, and cannot bear the weight placed on it against the plain teaching of 1 Timothy 2.
corruption_paragraphs: Two questions are involved and neither is settled in the way egalitarian readings require. The first is whether the name is Junia, a woman, or Junias, a man; the Authorized Version prints Junia, and the dictionary sees no need to dispute it. The second is what of note among the apostles means, and here the Greek can equally mean well known to the apostles rather than numbered among them — a reading held by Chrysostom’s critics and by many since. Even granting the inclusive sense, apostle in the New Testament often means a sent messenger of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25) rather than one of the Twelve. A single greeting in a list of salutations cannot overturn 1 Timothy 2:12 and 1 Timothy 3:1-7, which state the rule directly and give the reason from the creation order.

What Romans 9:3 shows is more worth dwelling on and is almost never preached. Paul, who had been stoned, beaten and hounded by his own countrymen, says he could wish himself accursed from Christ for their sake — the strongest thing a man could say, and only Moses in Exodus 32:32 says anything comparable. That is what love for the lost sounds like in an apostle, and it is stated about the very people who wanted him dead. Luke 14:12 gives the practical outworking for ordinary households: the Lord tells a host not to invite those who can repay him. Hospitality aimed at people who cannot return it is one of the few Christian practices whose motive cannot be mistaken.
roots_summary: Hebrew goel (H1350 participle), a kinsman-redeemer; gaal (H1350), to redeem, to act as kinsman; qarob (H7138), near, a near relative; Greek suggenes (G4773), a kinsman.
roots_lines: Hebrew goel — the kinsman-redeemer; the office Boaz fulfils in Ruth 4 and the type behind Christ’s redemption.
Hebrew gaal (H1350) — to redeem, to buy back as a kinsman; I know that my redeemer liveth (Job 19:25).
Hebrew qarob (H7138) — near, a near kinsman; any that is nigh of kin unto him (Leviticus 25:49).
Greek suggenes (G4773) — a relative, one of the same stock; my kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:3).
Greek lutrotes (G3086) — a redeemer, a ransomer; the New Testament term for the office Christ fills (Acts 7:35).
usage: My kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:3) — a man willing to be accursed for the people who hunted him.
Call not… thy kinsmen, nor thy rich neighbours (Luke 14:12) — hospitality aimed where it cannot be repaid.
Any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him (Leviticus 25:49) — the office of the kinsman-redeemer.

etymology: From Latin avunculus, a mother’s brother, through Old French oncle. Webster 1828: the brother of one’s father or mother. In the law of Leviticus the uncle is named among those with the right of redemption.
biblical_def: Uncle appears in Scripture chiefly in connection with duty rather than affection, because in Israel the relation carried legal weight. Leviticus places him in the order of redemption: Either his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself (Leviticus 25:49). A man sold into servitude was not left to his own resources; the family had a standing obligation, and the uncle stands near the head of the list. Jeremiah’s uncle brings him the strangest business proposition in Scripture: Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it (Jeremiah 32:7) — a field in a country under siege, offered to a prophet in prison, and bought as a sign that houses and fields would be possessed again. Esther’s guardian is named by the relation: Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter (Esther 2:15). And Saul’s uncle asks the question that exposes his nephew’s reticence about the kingdom (1 Samuel 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UNCLE as the brother of one’s father or mother; correlative to nephew or niece.
webster_full: UNCLE, n. — The brother of one’s father or mother; correlative to nephew or niece.
By extension, the husband of one’s aunt.
In the Hebrew law, one of the near kinsmen charged with the right and duty of redemption.
Also used loosely in Scripture of any near male relative of the parents’ generation.
From Latin avunculus, a mother’s brother, diminutive of avus, a grandfather.
scriptures: Leviticus 25:49
Either his uncle, or his uncle's son, may redeem him, or any that is nigh of kin unto him of his family may redeem him; or if he be able, he may redeem himself.
Jeremiah 32:7
Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it.
Esther 2:15

Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, was come to go in unto the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed. And Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her.
1 Samuel 10:14
And Saul's uncle said unto him and to his servant, Whither went ye? And he said, To seek the asses: and when we saw that they were no where, we came to Samuel.
corruption_summary: Leviticus 25 places the obligation to redeem an impoverished relative on the extended family by law, and the modern assumption that such duties belong to the state has quietly dissolved a structure Scripture treats as a divine ordinance.
corruption_paragraphs: The Levitical system is worth stating plainly because it is so foreign to modern arrangements. If a man became poor and sold himself, his brother, uncle, cousin, or any near kinsman may redeem him; if a man sold his land, the land returned at Jubilee regardless. The family, not the temple and not the crown, carried the obligation. Paul preserves the principle in the New Testament with unusual severity: if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1 Timothy 5:8), and he instructs churches not to charge themselves with widows who have children or nephews able to requite them. The dictionary holds family, church, and state as three God-ordained authorities with proper spheres; care for one’s own poor relations belongs first to the family, and a church or a state that assumes it wholesale does not thereby become more compassionate.

Jeremiah 32 is the finest illustration of what redemption of land meant in practice, and it is an act of faith staged as a legal transaction. The Babylonians were besieging Jerusalem, Jeremiah was shut up in the court of the prison for preaching that the city would fall, and his uncle’s son arrived to sell him a field in Anathoth. Jeremiah weighed out seventeen shekels of silver, signed the evidence, sealed it, took witnesses, and had the deeds put in an earthen vessel — and gave the reason: Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land. Faith bought a field it could not visit, from a family obligation it could have declined, in a country about to be emptied.
roots_summary: Hebrew dod (H1730), an uncle, a beloved one; dodah (H1733), an aunt; gaal (H1350), to redeem as kinsman; Greek anepsios (G431), a cousin.
roots_lines: Hebrew dod (H1730) — an uncle, and also a beloved; the same word is the beloved of the Song of Solomon.
Hebrew dodah (H1733) — an aunt; the feminine of dod (Exodus 6:20).
Hebrew gaal (H1350) — to redeem, to act the part of a kinsman; the verb of Leviticus 25:49.
Hebrew geullah (H1353) — the right of redemption; the right of redemption is thine to buy it (Jeremiah 32:7).
Greek anepsios (G431) — a cousin; Marcus, sister’s son to Barnabas (Colossians 4:10).
usage: Either his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him (Leviticus 25:49) — redemption as a standing family obligation.
Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth (Jeremiah 32:7) — a field bought under siege as a sign of return.
Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai (Esther 2:15) — an orphan raised as a daughter by her father’s brother.

etymology: From Old French espouser, from Latin sponsare, from spondere, to promise solemnly. Webster 1828: betrothed; promised in marriage. In Hebrew practice betrothal was legally binding and could be dissolved only by divorce, which is why Joseph considered putting Mary away privily.
biblical_def: Espoused means betrothed, and the reader who supposes it means engaged in the modern sense will misread the nativity. Betrothal in Israel was a binding covenant: the parties were husband and wife in law before they came together, unfaithfulness during it was adultery, and it was dissolved only by a writ of divorce. So Matthew writes: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:18), and Joseph, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily. Luke uses the same term twice — To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary (Luke 1:27), and, at Bethlehem, To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child (Luke 2:5). And Paul takes the whole institution as the figure of his ministry to a church: I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). The apostle is the friend of the bridegroom, and his anxiety is that the bride reach the wedding undefiled.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ESPOUSED as betrothed; promised or engaged in marriage by contract; also, taken up or embraced, as a cause or an opinion.
webster_full: ESPOUSED, pp. — Betrothed; promised in marriage by contract; affianced.
United in marriage; wedded.
Embraced; taken as one’s own; as, to have espoused a cause or an opinion.
In Hebrew usage, betrothal was a binding covenant which only a writ of divorce could dissolve.
From Latin spondeo, to promise solemnly — the root also of spouse, sponsor, and respond.
scriptures: Matthew 1:18
Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.
Luke 1:27
To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary.
Luke 2:5
To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child.
2 Corinthians 11:2
For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
corruption_summary: The virgin birth is the first Christian doctrine that liberal theology abandoned, treated as a legend borrowed from pagan birth stories, and the espousal texts are precisely where the historical claim is anchored.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew and Luke both state it, independently and in different registers, and both anchor it in a legal situation with named parties. Mary was espoused to Joseph; before they came together she was found with child; Joseph, a just man, resolved on quiet divorce until an angel told him otherwise; and Luke records Mary’s own question, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man? The comparison with pagan tales of gods begetting children on women fails at the point that matters: those are stories of physical union, and this narrative has none. Isaiah 7:14 had said a virgin shall conceive, and Matthew cites it. Christologically the doctrine is not optional: the One conceived must be truly man to stand in man’s place and truly God to bear the wrath, and Luke 1:35 gives the reason for the manner — therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.

2 Corinthians 11:2 draws the practical consequence for the church, and Paul’s emotion in it is worth noticing. He says he is jealous over you with godly jealousy — a jealousy he ascribes to God and claims for himself — because he has espoused the Corinthians to one husband. The very next verse names the danger: as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. A minister’s doctrinal vigilance is here presented not as pedantry but as the jealousy of a man responsible to deliver a bride intact, and the corruption feared is not gross immorality but a subtle shifting away from simplicity toward another Jesus.
roots_summary: Greek mnesteuo (G3423), to betroth, to espouse; harmozo (G718), to join, to betroth; Hebrew aras (H781), to betroth; kelulah (H3623), espousals.
roots_lines: Greek mnesteuo (G3423) — to betroth; used of Mary in Matthew 1:18, Luke 1:27 and Luke 2:5.
Greek harmozo (G718) — to join, to fit together, to betroth; I have espoused you to one husband (2 Corinthians 11:2).
Hebrew aras (H781) — to betroth; I will betroth thee unto me for ever (Hosea 2:19).
Hebrew kelulah (H3623) — espousals, betrothal; the love of thine espousals (Jeremiah 2:2).
Greek parthenos (G3933) — a virgin; a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2) and the virgin of Matthew 1:23.
usage: His mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together (Matthew 1:18) — a binding covenant, not a modern engagement.
Mary his espoused wife, being great with child (Luke 2:5) — the legal status Luke is careful to state.
I have espoused you to one husband (2 Corinthians 11:2) — the apostle as the friend of the bridegroom.

etymology: From Old French surnom, from Latin super (over, above) and nomen (name). Webster 1828: an additional name; a name added to the baptismal or first name. In Scripture the surnaming is usually God’s act or the apostles’, and it says what a man is or will be.
biblical_def: Surname in Scripture is rarely a family name in the modern sense; it is an added name that declares something. God claims the act for Himself in one of the most striking verses about Cyrus, a pagan king named a century and a half before his birth: For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me (Isaiah 45:4). God names and titles a man who does not know Him, and uses him to send Israel home. The apostles surname a generous Levite from Cyprus, and the name outlasts the original: And Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation,) a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus (Acts 4:36). Luke uses the word plainly of a man’s second name in the message to Cornelius: call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter (Acts 10:5) — itself a surname the Lord had given him. And again of the evangelist: the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark (Acts 12:12), the young man who left Paul in Pamphylia and whom Paul later called profitable to him for the ministry.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SURNAME as an additional name; a name or appellation added to the baptismal or Christian name, and become the family name; also, an appellation added to the original name from some quality, achievement, or circumstance.
webster_full: SURNAME, n. — An additional name; a name added to the baptismal or first name.
The family name, borne in common by the members of a household or line.
An appellation added from a quality, an achievement, or a place; as, Simon, surnamed Peter.
SURNAME, v.t. — To name or call by an appellation added to the original name.
From Latin super, over, and nomen, a name — the root also of nominate and renown.
scriptures: Isaiah 45:4
For Jacob my servant's sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me.
Acts 4:36
And Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation,) a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus,
Acts 10:5
And now send men to Joppa, and call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter:
Acts 12:12
And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 45 names Cyrus a century and a half before his birth, and the critical scholarship that invented a second and third Isaiah did so principally to avoid that fact.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument for dividing the book is presented as literary and historical, but its engine is the Cyrus oracle. Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1 name Cyrus, call him God’s shepherd and His anointed, and describe his conquest of Babylon and his decree to rebuild the temple — and Cyrus was born some hundred and fifty years after Isaiah prophesied. If predictive prophecy of this kind is ruled out in advance, the chapters must have been written by an exilic author, and so Deutero-Isaiah was posited. The dictionary rejects the division outright and holds one prophet Isaiah. The New Testament quotes from both halves and attributes them to Isaiah by name, including John 12:38-41, which cites Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 6 in consecutive breaths and says These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him.

The Cyrus text also says something the church needs about God’s use of unbelieving rulers. I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me — and two verses on, I girded thee, though thou hast not known me. God titles, equips, and directs a Persian king who did not worship Him, for the sake of Jacob His servant. That is neither an endorsement of Cyrus nor a claim that he was secretly godly; it is the doctrine of providence applied to politics, and it should steady Christians who alternately baptise and despair over the rulers of their own moment. Acts 4:36 shows the gentler side of naming: the apostles called a man the son of consolation, and the church has called him that for two thousand years because it fitted.
roots_summary: Hebrew kanah (H3655), to give a title, to surname; shem (H8034), a name; Greek epikaleo (G1941), to surname, to call upon; eponomazo (G2028), to name after.
roots_lines: Hebrew kanah (H3655) — to address by an additional name, to give a title of honour; I have surnamed thee (Isaiah 45:4).
Hebrew shem (H8034) — a name; in Hebrew thought a name expresses the nature or destiny of the bearer.
Greek epikaleo (G1941) — to surname, to call by an added name; Simon, whose surname is Peter (Acts 10:5).
Greek Barnabas (G921) — interpreted by Luke as son of consolation, from Aramaic bar, son, and a root of prophecy or exhortation.
Greek paraklesis (G3874) — consolation, exhortation; the word Luke uses to render the meaning of Barnabas.
usage: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me (Isaiah 45:4) — a pagan king titled by God a century before his birth.
Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas (Acts 4:36) — a name that fitted, and outlasted the original.
Call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter (Acts 10:5) — itself a name the Lord had given.

etymology: From own, Saxon agan, to possess. Webster 1828: the rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title. Scripture uses the word in case law about liability, in a prophet’s rebuke, and at the entry into Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Owner in Scripture appears where responsibility is being fixed. The case law of Exodus makes ownership a matter of liability rather than mere possession: If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be quit (Exodus 21:28) — and the following verse withdraws the acquittal if the owner had been warned and did not keep the animal in. God’s law distinguishes between accident and negligence, and holds a man answerable for what he owns. Isaiah opens his prophecy with the word in a rebuke that has never lost its sting: The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master’s crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider (Isaiah 1:3). Beasts recognise the man who feeds them; the covenant nation did not recognise God. Luke records the owners of a colt watching it taken: as they were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt? (Luke 19:33) — and the answer, the Lord hath need of him, was enough. And Acts 27:11 shows a centurion trusting the ship’s owner over the apostle, to the loss of the ship.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OWNER as the rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title, whether he is the possessor or not — noting that the owner and the possessor may be different persons.
webster_full: OWNER, n. — The rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title to a thing.
Webster observes that the owner of a thing is not always the possessor, for the possessor may hold it wrongfully.
OWN, v.t. — To have the legal or rightful title to; to possess by right.
Also, to acknowledge as belonging to oneself; to avow; to confess — as, to own a fault.
From Saxon agan, to possess — the root also of own, owe, and ought.
scriptures: Exodus 21:28
If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be quit.
Isaiah 1:3
The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider.
Luke 19:33
And as they were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt?
Acts 27:11
Nevertheless the centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul.
corruption_summary: Scripture treats private property as real and protected while making the owner answerable to God for what he holds, which cuts against both the collectivism that denies ownership and the absolutism that treats property as beyond moral claim.
corruption_paragraphs: The eighth and tenth commandments presuppose property: there is no theft if nothing is owned, and no coveting of a neighbour’s goods if he has none. Naboth’s refusal to sell his vineyard to a king is upheld by God and Ahab’s seizure judged. Peter says to Ananias of his land, whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? — the sin was the lie, not the ownership. So the collectivist claim that property is theft has no purchase here. But the owner is not sovereign over what he owns. The earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof (Psalm 24:1); the land in Israel could not be permanently sold because the land is mine (Leviticus 25:23); gleanings belonged to the poor by law; and Exodus 21:29 makes a man liable for the harm his property does when he was warned and did nothing. Ownership under God is stewardship with title.

Isaiah 1:3 turns the word into the sharpest rebuke in the prophets, and it works by comparison with animals. An ox knows the man who feeds it; a donkey knows its master’s crib; Israel does not know its owner and does not consider. The failure is not intellectual but relational, and the chapter goes on to describe a people busy with sacrifices, new moons and appointed feasts that God says His soul hates. Religious activity had continued while recognition of God had stopped. That is a diagnosis a busy and well-attended church should read slowly, since nothing in Isaiah 1 suggests that the offerings had declined.
roots_summary: Hebrew baal (H1167), an owner, a lord, a husband; qanah (H7069), to acquire, to buy; Greek kurios (G2962), lord, owner; naukleros (G3490), a shipowner.
roots_lines: Hebrew baal (H1167) — an owner, master, husband; the owner of the ox shall be quit (Exodus 21:28).
Hebrew qanah (H7069) — to get, to acquire, to buy; behind the ox knoweth his owner (Isaiah 1:3).
Greek kurios (G2962) — lord, owner, master; the owners thereof said unto them (Luke 19:33), and the church’s title for Christ.
Greek naukleros (G3490) — a shipowner; the master and the owner of the ship (Acts 27:11).
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward; the New Testament’s standing description of a believer’s relation to what he holds.
usage: The owner of the ox shall be quit (Exodus 21:28) — liability distinguished from accident, and fixed on the owner.
The ox knoweth his owner… but Israel doth not know (Isaiah 1:3) — the sharpest comparison in the prophets.
The owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt? (Luke 19:33) — and the Lord hath need of him was enough.
